name: Design a Distributed File System
intent: Store petabytes of very large files on thousands of cheap servers that fail every day, with one metadata master, big replicated chunks, and no lost data.
codeTitle: a mini chunk store with racks, heartbeats, re-replication and scrubbing
finalIntro: A client appends to a file, a server dies, and the cluster repairs itself.
prompt: Design a distributed file system in the style of GFS or HDFS. Applications write huge files (logs, crawled pages, training data) and read them back in large streams. The cluster has thousands of commodity servers in many racks, and some of them fail every day. The system must keep every byte safe and keep working while hardware breaks.
functional: Create, delete, list and rename files in a directory tree
Append to a file and write to it, with many clients writing at once
Read any part of a file, mostly in long sequential streams
Keep files safe across disk, server and rack failures
Take consistent snapshots of a directory tree
nonFunctional: Hold tens of petabytes and hundreds of millions of files
Give high total throughput, since big streaming reads and appends matter more than low latency
Lose no data when a disk, a server or a whole rack fails, and repair within minutes to hours
Keep serving reads and writes while servers fail, and recover from a master crash within a minute
Detect silent disk corruption before the last good copy is gone
Run on cheap hardware, so failure is the normal case rather than the exception

firstAttempt.text: One big file server (or a network-attached disk array) with a local file system. Every client mounts it and reads and writes files over the network. For safety, a nightly backup copies everything to a second machine.
limits: The capacity and the bandwidth of a single machine are a hard ceiling, far below petabytes
When the machine fails, everything is unavailable until it is repaired or restored
A nightly backup means a day of data can be lost, and restoring petabytes takes days
Every read and write passes through one network card and one CPU
Silent disk corruption is copied into the backup without anyone noticing

steps.title: Split files into big chunks, and keep the map in a master
steps.problem: A single machine cannot hold or serve petabytes, and a file system whose every read goes through one server cannot scale.
steps.fix: Cut every file into large fixed-size chunks, for example 64 or 128 MB, and spread the chunks over many chunkservers, each storing its chunks as ordinary local files. One master keeps the metadata: the directory tree, the list of chunks of each file, and which servers hold each chunk. A client asks the master only where the data is, then reads and writes the chunkservers directly, so file data never passes through the master. The client also caches the answer for a while.
steps.tradeoff: Total throughput grows with the number of servers, and the master handles small metadata requests rather than bulk data. Big chunks keep the metadata small and make streaming efficient, but they suit big files and give small files a poor deal. The master is now a single point that every client depends on.

steps.title: Replicate each chunk across racks
steps.problem: With thousands of commodity servers, disks and machines fail every day, and a whole rack can drop when its switch or power fails. A single copy of a chunk is a lost chunk.
steps.fix: Keep three copies of every chunk by default. Placement is rack-aware: the first copy goes on one server, the second on a server in a different rack, and the third on another server in that same second rack. Any single server failure and any single rack failure leaves at least one copy. The master spreads new chunks towards less full servers and avoids putting many new chunks on a server that was just added.
steps.tradeoff: Data survives a rack, and reads can go to the nearest copy. Raw storage cost is three times the data, and the cross-rack copy uses scarce bandwidth. Putting two copies in one rack is a deliberate compromise between safety and network cost.

steps.title: Write through a pipeline, and let a primary order the writes
steps.problem: Many clients can write to the same chunk at once, and all three copies must apply the writes in the same order, without sending every byte through the master.
steps.fix: The master gives one replica of the chunk a lease of about 60 seconds, which makes it the primary. A client first pushes its data along a chain: to the nearest replica, which forwards to the next as it receives, so every server's outbound bandwidth is used and the client sends the data once. Then the client tells the primary to write. The primary gives the write a serial number, applies it, and tells the secondaries to apply the writes in that same order. When all reply, the client is told it worked. Leases are renewed in heartbeats and expire by themselves if the primary dies.
steps.tradeoff: Data flow and control flow are separated, so the network is used fully and the master stays out of the data path. If a write fails on one replica, that region can be left inconsistent and the client must retry, so appends are at least once and readers have to cope with duplicates and padding.

steps.title: Detect dead servers with heartbeats, and re-replicate
steps.problem: Servers die all the time. Each death leaves thousands of chunks with only two copies, and a second failure before they are fixed could lose the last copy of some of them.
steps.fix: Every chunkserver sends the master a heartbeat every few seconds, carrying its list of chunks, which is how the master learns the chunk map in the first place. A server silent for some minutes is declared dead. The master then finds every chunk that is below its target, puts them in a queue ordered by how few copies remain, and instructs servers to copy them. Chunks down to one copy go first, copying is throttled so it does not starve normal traffic, and the new copies obey the rack rule.
steps.tradeoff: The cluster heals itself without an operator, and the time at risk is bounded by the copy rate, because every other server helps in parallel. A long timeout avoids copying data for a server that only rebooted, and a short one shortens the risk window. A dead rack causes a wave of copying that competes with applications.

steps.title: Make the master durable, replaceable, and small
steps.problem: The master holds all the metadata in memory, and every client depends on it. If it crashes, the file system is gone. Its memory also caps how many files can exist, and small files make that worse.
steps.fix: Every change to the namespace is first written to an operation log, which is replicated to several disks and to a standby master before the client is answered. The master takes a checkpoint of its state from time to time, so recovery loads the latest checkpoint and replays a short tail of the log. Chunk locations are not logged, since chunkservers report them on startup. A standby or shadow master follows the log and takes over in about a minute through leader election, and can already serve reads. To keep the master small, chunks are large, tiny files are packed into container files, and very big clusters split the namespace over several masters.
steps.tradeoff: The master stops being a single point of data loss, and metadata operations stay very fast because they are in memory. Memory is still the hard limit of one master, about 150 bytes per file and per chunk, so a billion tiny files is a problem, and failover must make sure the old master really stopped before the new one writes.

steps.title: Checksum every block, and scrub in the background
steps.problem: Disks silently flip bits. A chunk may look healthy on a quiet server for months, and then the other copies are gone before anyone notices that this one is wrong.
steps.fix: Each chunk is split into 64 KB blocks, and every block has a 32-bit checksum stored next to the data. A chunkserver verifies the checksum on every read, and returns an error rather than bad data. The client reads another replica, and the master schedules a fresh copy and deletes the bad one. A background scrubber also reads cold chunks slowly, so damage is found while the other copies are still good. Checksums are computed again at the point of writing, and when data is copied during re-replication.
steps.tradeoff: Silent corruption becomes a normal, repaired event, and cold data is verified before it is needed. Checksums cost a little CPU and a few bytes per block, and the scrubber uses disk bandwidth, so it is rate-limited and run at quiet times.

failures.impact: Thousands of chunks drop from three copies to two, and reads of those chunks must use other replicas.
failures.answer: Clients retry on another replica from the list the master gave them. After the heartbeat timeout the master declares the server dead and queues its chunks for re-replication. All the other servers copy in parallel, so tens of terabytes are restored in minutes rather than hours.

failures.scenario: A rack loses its switch or power
failures.impact: Dozens of servers vanish together, and some chunks lose two of their three copies at the same time.
failures.answer: Rack-aware placement guarantees every chunk has a copy in another rack, so nothing is lost. The master puts chunks with a single copy at the front of the queue and copies them first, with the rate limited so applications still get bandwidth. Without the rack rule, a few chunks would have all three copies in that rack.

failures.impact: No client can open, create or find files, and writes to new chunks stop.
failures.answer: The standby master has followed the operation log and takes over within about a minute, using the checkpoint and the log tail. Chunkservers re-announce their chunk lists. Clients that cached chunk locations keep reading and writing during the gap. The old master must be fenced so it cannot still write to the log.

failures.scenario: A job writes a hundred million tiny files
failures.impact: The master runs out of memory long before the disks fill, and every metadata operation gets slow.
failures.answer: Each file costs the master about as much as a huge file, so the answer is to avoid tiny files: pack them into larger container files (sequence files, archives or a table format) with an index, set quotas on the number of files per directory, and move to a federated namespace if the cluster as a whole really needs more objects than one master can hold.

failures.scenario: A disk flips a bit in a rarely read chunk
failures.impact: One copy is wrong, and if it stays undiscovered until two others are lost, the bad data may be the only copy left.
failures.answer: The block checksum fails when the scrubber reads it. The chunkserver reports the chunk to the master, which marks that replica bad, creates a new copy from a healthy replica and deletes the damaged one. Reads that meet the bad block earlier fall back to another replica in the same way.

failures.scenario: The primary dies in the middle of a write
failures.impact: Some replicas applied the write and others did not, so the copies of that region now differ.
failures.answer: The client sees an error and retries the write. Until the old lease expires, the master will not give a new primary, which prevents two primaries ordering writes at once. The inconsistent region is marked, readers skip duplicate and padding records using record ids and checksums, and the client's retry lands at a fresh offset.

alternatives.title: How to keep the metadata

options.name: One master with everything in memory
options.pro: Simple, strongly consistent and very fast, with global knowledge for placement
options.con: Limited by one machine's memory, and a failover to cover

options.name: A federated set of masters, each owning part of the namespace
options.pro: Raises the number of files that fit, and isolates teams
options.con: Cross-directory renames are hard and the load is uneven

options.name: Metadata in a distributed database
options.pro: Scales to billions of files without a size limit
options.con: Each metadata operation is slower and the system is more complex

alternatives.pick: One in-memory master with a log and a standby, which is enough for very large clusters. Federate or move to a database store when file counts reach billions.

alternatives.title: How to be safe against failure

options.name: Three full copies
options.pro: Simple, fast reads, and easy and quick repair by copying

options.name: Erasure coding, for example 6 data and 3 parity blocks
options.pro: Survives any three losses with only 1.5 times the storage
options.con: Reads of a lost block and repairs need many other blocks, and small writes are costly

alternatives.pick: Copies for hot and new data, and erasure coding for cold data, where storage cost matters and reads are rare.

alternatives.title: How big a chunk is

options.name: Small, about 4 MB
options.pro: Good for small files and finer load balancing
options.con: Many more chunks, so the master's memory and its traffic grow 16 to 32 times

options.name: Large, 64 to 256 MB
options.pro: Little metadata, long sequential transfers, and clients that rarely contact the master
options.con: Small files waste a chunk's bookkeeping, and a hot small file can overload its few servers

alternatives.pick: 128 MB, with small files packed together and hot files given more copies.

alternatives.title: What guarantees writes give

options.name: Strict POSIX semantics
options.con: Needs distributed locking and strict ordering that cost throughput

options.name: Relaxed semantics with atomic record append
options.pro: Many writers can append to one file with no coordination, which is what logs and pipelines need
options.con: Readers must tolerate duplicates and padding, and applications have to be written for it

alternatives.pick: Relaxed semantics with record append, since the workloads are append-heavy and write-once.

roles.label: Applications
roles.description: Programs and jobs that read and write files.

roles.label: Master
roles.description: The namespace, the chunk map and the leases.

roles.label: Operation log
roles.description: The durable record of metadata changes, and the standby that follows it.

roles.label: Chunkservers
roles.description: The servers and racks that store the chunks.

quiz.question: A single file server with a 10 Gbit/s network card (about 1.25 GB/s) holds all training data. A job now needs about 100 GB/s of aggregate reads. Which redesign scales to that?
options: Add a second 10 Gbit/s card and a faster disk array, repeating the upgrade as the demand grows
Split files into large chunks on many servers, and let clients ask a master where they are, then read directly
Run eight full copies of the file server behind a load balancer, so each one takes an eighth of the reads
Send all reads through a master that fetches the data from the chunk servers, so it can order and cache them
quiz.explanation: Throughput grows with the number of servers when data flows straight from many chunkservers to clients, and the master only answers small location questions. Copies of one server and bigger cards hit a ceiling far below 100 GB/s, and a master in the data path becomes the bottleneck.

quiz.question: A master keeps metadata in RAM at about 150 bytes per file and 150 bytes per chunk, and has 64 GB. A pipeline writes 400 million files of about 100 KB each, one chunk per file. Disk space is ample. Which change fixes the real limit?
options: Lower the chunk size to 4 MB, so each small file fits into its chunk without wasted space
Add more chunkservers with large disks, because storing 40 TB of data needs far more raw capacity than today
Use two replicas instead of three for these files, which cuts the number of chunk entries by a third
Pack the small files into container files of about 128 MB with an index, so the master tracks fewer objects
quiz.explanation: Files plus chunks come to about 800 million entries, or 120 GB, which is more than the master's RAM, while the 40 TB of data is no problem. Packing cuts the object count by a factor of about a thousand. A smaller chunk size adds chunks, and fewer replicas does not remove file entries.

quiz.question: A cluster holds 20 PB of logs. For the first 30 days they are read heavily, after that about once a month. They must survive the loss of any two servers. Which storage policy is the best fit?
options: Use 6+3 erasure coding from the first day, since it uses only 1.5 times the space instead of 3 times
Keep 3 copies for ever, since repair by copying is simple and fast, and disks are cheap enough for this
Keep 3 copies for 30 days, then re-encode to erasure coding such as 6 data and 3 parity blocks
Keep 3 copies for 30 days, then drop to 2 copies, which saves a third of the space and survives a rack loss
quiz.explanation: Hot data wants plain copies for fast reads and cheap repair, and cold data wants the 1.5x cost of erasure coding that still survives three losses. Starting with erasure coding makes the heavy early reads and repairs touch many blocks. Two copies survive only one loss, not the required two.
